chapter: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
title: Meeting King Pleasure and writing lyrics to Don't Get Scared
summary: King Pleasure invited him to record Don't Get Scared and let him write his own words for the Lars Gullin solo.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Had you met – when did you meet King Pleasure?

I met him when he – I was in the Turf bar at 52nd and Broadway. We all used to hang out in there, all the songwriters and performers. He came in. Somebody introduced me to him. I said, “Oh man.” I said, “You started me writing like that.” He says, “Yeah. That’s what I want to talk to you about.” I says, “What is that?” He says, “I’d like you to record something with me.” He says, “I have this Stan Getz tune that he recorded in Sweden called Don’t Get Scared.
“When you see danger facing you, little boy don’t get scared.”

I liked him, because he was not only a handsome man, but he was very intelligent and a well-spoken man, and very artistic. He did something that is unprecedented in my whole life. I’ve never seen anybody do that.

He gave me the words to Don’t Get Scared, and there were no words to my solo, the Lars Gullin baritone saxophone solo. I said, “Where are the words to Lars Gullin’s part?” He said, “You write them yourself.” I never knew an artist to do that.
Just give you the liberty of . . .
To give me the liberty of writing my own lyrics to what was his record date and his project. That was so big-hearted. I’ve never encountered it since.
I love that song, and I don’t . . .
There’s a little portion of it that I don’t understand.
It says something like, “Life is very funny every way. Got to ha-ha-ha-ha every day. Never be afraid. Now I know you’ve never read, but remember what I said. Any one so . . .”
“Anyone so tender he would easily surrender his all.” [Hendricks sings:] “I’m so sorry for him” – the little fellow – “but he’s better off dead.”
